media.title: Quilt Lace
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Quilt Lace

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration
- Textbook source: Grandmother's Quilt, the opening story with the red, green and blue lace reels of 40, 50 and 25 units. The quilt is 15 patches by 10 patches, counted from the picture. Practice values added by the plan: a quilt of 7 by 5 patches, and a quilt of 10 by 8 patches with reels of 30, 36 and 40 units (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that lace for a border must go all the way round the quilt, and finds how long it must be by adding the units along the four sides.
- Out of scope: the word "perimeter" (the video that follows names it), area, any length rule, rectangles as a topic.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- The stage shows Grandmother's quilt cover spread on a wooden floor, seen from above, filling most of the stage: 15 patches along the long side and 10 along the short side, each patch about 48 px across on a laptop. Below it, in a row, lie three ribbon reels about 90 px wide with a white label on each rim: red "40 units", green "50 units", blue "25 units".
- Instruction line: "Which lace will go all the way round the quilt? Tap your guess."
- Each reel gives one small hop to show it can be tapped.

2. Scene and Objects
- Background: a plain warm wooden floor of wide planks, photo, top view, no clutter.
- Quilt: drawn in code so the count is exact, 150 patches in rows from the top: green, red, yellow, green, red, yellow, green, red, yellow, green. Green patches have small dots, red patches a white weave, yellow patches spirals. Thin dark seams between patches and a pink frilled rim all round. One patch side is 1 unit.
- Lace: a ribbon 12 px thick in the colour of its reel, lying along the outer edge of the patches on the rim, with a small tick at every unit and a longer tick at every 5 units. It is pulled out of its reel, so the reel shrinks as lace is used.
- Reels: photo cut-outs of ribbon reels in red, green and blue.
- Chips on the stage: the goal chip of the activity (top left) and "Units laid: 0" (top right, counts up while laying).

3. Main Interaction
- Tap a reel to pick it: it lifts and its loose end goes to the top left corner of the quilt. Only one lace is out at a time; tapping another reel puts the first one back.
- Drag the lace tip clockwise along the border. The tip follows the finger's distance along the border, snaps to whole units, one unit for each patch side, and turns at the corners. Dragging back takes the lace back one unit at a time. When the reel is empty the lace stops and its loose end shows a flat cut end.
- Practice quilts: every outer edge is a small bar; tap a bar to count it (it turns orange, the counter goes up by 1), or drag a finger along the rim to count the bars it passes. A bar is counted once only. Tap a patch to mark it (it glows orange).
- Bottom buttons (at most 3): Hint, Reset (picks up the lace and the counts of this activity), and Check, which becomes Next when the activity is done.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Lay each lace along the border and see where it ends." Goal chip: "Try all 3 laces". Setup: quilt 15 by 10, reels 40, 50 and 25 units. Guess: before laying, the child taps the reel they think goes all the way round; it gets a flag "my guess". The child picks each reel in turn, in any order, and drags its tip round from the top left corner. Result: the red lace stops at the bottom left corner after 15 + 10 + 15 = 40 units, strip: "The red lace has 40 units. It stops at the corner and 10 units are still to cover." The blue lace stops at the bottom right corner after 15 + 10 = 25 units, strip: "The blue lace has 25 units. 25 units are still to cover." The green lace meets its own start: the quilt glows, labels 15, 10, 15 and 10 appear on the four sides and the strip says "15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50. The border is 50 units, so the 50 unit green lace fits exactly." The guess flag turns green on the green reel and grey on another. The goal chip turns green when all 3 are tried. Help: guided, ticks on the lace, corners flash when passed, the running count is always visible.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Tap every edge on the outside of the quilt." Goal chip: "Count the border". Setup: a small practice quilt of 7 by 5 patches (practice values) with 24 outer bars. Guess: "How many units is the border? Tap one: 12, 24 or 35." The child taps or sweeps over the outer bars until all 24 are counted. Result: the guess chip is compared; the four sides label themselves 7, 5, 7, 5 and the strip says "7 + 5 + 7 + 5 = 24. The border is 24 units." A plain note shows what the guess was, for example "You guessed 12. That is only one long side and one short side." Help: guided, the bars are drawn and the counter is shown.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Tap the patches on the border. Then compare with the lace units." Goal chip: "Patches or units". Setup: the same 7 by 5 quilt, no bars, no labels. Guess: "Are the border patches and the lace units the same number? Tap Same or Different." The child taps every patch that touches the outside edge, 20 patches, counter "Border patches: 20". Result: the 4 corner patches pulse with a small "2 edges" tag, strip: "20 patches but 24 units. Each corner patch has 2 edges on the border: 20 + 4 = 24. Count units of lace, not patches." Help: independent, only the goal chip.
- Star Challenge 1 (practice values). Goal line: "Tick every lace that is long enough to go all the way round." Goal chip: "Long enough". Setup: a new quilt of 10 patches by 8 patches and three reels labelled purple "30 units", orange "36 units" and teal "40 units". Guess and do: the child ticks the reels they think are long enough, then presses Check; the tool lays each ticked lace round the border. Success condition: exactly the orange 36 and the teal 40 are ticked. Result: the orange lace closes the loop, the teal lace closes it with 4 units left over and scissors cut them off, the purple lace stops 6 units short, strip: "10 + 8 + 10 + 8 = 36. The border is 36 units. The 36 lace fits exactly and the 40 lace is long enough with 4 units to spare. The 30 lace is 6 units short." Help: independent. Retry is free and the ticks stay.

5. Mathematical Understanding
- By laying lace, running out and counting units on each side, the child sees that the lace needed is every side added together, and that it must go all the way round with no gap.
- By counting bars and then patches, the child sees that the corners are the trap: a corner patch has two edges on the border, so units are not patches.
- Rules in the child's words: "The lace must go all the way round." "Add the units along every side." "A longer lace also works." "Count units, not patches."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the strip turns green and shows the one-line why, the finished quilt glows once. Wrong answer: red strip, small shake, one friendly line; retry is free, no scores. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Guess steps are never marked wrong. After the result a plain strip compares: "You guessed X. The answer is Y."
- Mistake: taps a seam inside the quilt -> red strip, small shake: "That edge is inside the quilt. Count only the edges on the outside." The outer rim lights up.
- Mistake: taps an edge twice -> "You counted this edge already." The bar blinks once.
- Mistake: lets go of the lace away from the border -> the tip waits at the last unit: "Keep the lace on the border."
- Mistake in Challenge 1: ticks the purple 30 -> "The 30 lace stops 6 units short of the corner. It is not long enough." Leaves out the teal 40 -> "The 40 lace is longer than the border, so it works too. The extra can be cut off." The reel in question pulses.
- Hints, three levels (Activities 1 to 3 and Challenge): (1) "Where does the lace start, and where does it have to end?" or, in Activity 3, "Which patches touch the outside?" (2) the four corners glow one after the other, or the outer rim lights; (3) "The long side is 15 units and the short side is 10 units. How many long sides and short sides are there? Add them all." For the small quilts the numbers 7 and 5, or 10 and 8, are used in the same words.
- Edge cases: a lace exactly as long as the border (50 on 50) closes the loop and the start and end meet; a lace longer than the border leaves extra that is cut; a lace that stops exactly at a corner (blue, red) still has whole sides left; a corner unit is counted once when the lace turns.

7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is described above; it is finished when the correct reels are ticked and checked.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "The lace must go all the way round the border." "Add the units along every side to find how much lace you need." "Count units of lace, not patches." Think and talk: "A lace is longer than the border. What can you do with the extra lace?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: top-view wooden plank floor photo; three photo cut-outs of ribbon reels (red, green, blue) plus the same reel shape recoloured purple, orange and teal for the challenge; fabric swatch textures for green dots, red weave and yellow spirals; pink frilled rim strip; small scissors cut-out for the challenge. Quilts, bars, ticks and counters are drawn in code.
- Language: English only, short sentences, the units are the word "units". Nothing on screen says perimeter.

tool_config.idea: Find out by laying lace along the border of a quilt that the lace needed is the length all the way round, counted in units: the red and blue reels run out, the green reel fits exactly, and two laces of different colours can share the border. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the perimeter.
tool_config.title: Quilt Lace
tool_config.screen: Grandmother's sunny patchwork room, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The quilt cover is spread on the floor and is the largest thing on screen: 15 patches along the long side and 10 patches along the short side in rows of green, red and yellow patches with a pink rim, as in your maths book. Every patch side is 1 unit. On a stool beside the quilt stand three lace reels with the lengths of your maths book: red lace 40 units, green lace 50 units and blue lace 25 units, each lace marked in units. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a reel to pick its lace; drag the end of the lace along the border of the quilt, and it snaps to the patch edges, one unit for each patch side, and turns at the corners; a Cut button that cuts the lace at the place reached; an Undo button that picks the lace up one unit at a time; a Two laces switch that gives a second reel slot, so that a second colour can be laid after the first one is cut; Check, Hint, Retry (picks up the lace of this step), Reset (returns the quilt and the three reels), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a counter units laid (for example 25), the units left to cover (for example 25 left), the length of the reel chosen, and a card number out of 7. On the small practice quilt the student taps each outer edge and a counter adds one for each tap.
feedback: The lace follows the finger along the patch edges and the counter units laid goes up one for each patch side. When a reel runs out the lace stops with a soft note, for example: The red lace has 40 units. The border is longer, 10 units still to cover.
When a lace goes all the way round exactly, the quilt shines softly and the tool names the sides: 15, 10, 15 and 10 units.

A tap on an outer edge of the practice quilt lights it orange and adds one to the counter. An edge that is inside the quilt gives a soft amber note: This edge is inside. Count the edges on the outside.

In the two-lace challenge the tool accepts any split that covers the whole border, and says for example: 30 units of red and 20 units of blue make 50 units, the whole border. If the lace is too long for a reel it says: The blue reel has only 25 units.
A wrong tick shows a soft amber note and never a red cross, and it asks the student to lay that lace along the border and look again.
tool_config.done_when: The student has laid the red, blue and green laces along the border and seen which one is long enough, has counted the border of the small quilt edge by edge, has seen why the patches on the border are fewer than the units of lace, and has ticked the right lace and cut two laces for the border.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: pick the blue lace and drag it along the border from the top left corner. Where does it run out? Answer: after 25 units, at the bottom right corner, because the top side is 15 units and the right side is 10 units and 15 + 10 = 25. The bottom side and the left side are not covered, so the blue lace is too short.

Card 2: pick the red lace and lay it the same way. Where does it run out? Answer: after 40 units, at the bottom left corner, because 15 + 10 + 15 = 40. The left side, 10 units, is still not covered, so the red lace is too short.
Card 3: pick the green lace and lay it all the way round. What do the four sides add up to? Answer: 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 units. The green lace is 50 units, so it fits all the way round exactly.
Card 4 (practice values): a small quilt of 6 patches by 4 patches. Tap every outer edge once and read the counter. Answer: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20, so the border has 20 units.

Card 5: count the patches along the border of the big quilt, then count the units of lace. Why are the two numbers different? Answer: the patches on the border are 46 and the lace units are 50, because each of the 4 corner patches has 2 sides on the border but is counted once as a patch: 46 + 4 = 50. Count the units of lace, not the patches.

Challenge: 'Tick the lace option that would cover the entire border of the quilt. (i) Red lace 40 units (ii) Green lace 50 units (iii) Blue lace 25 units.' Lay each lace and tick the one that covers the entire border. Answer: (ii) the green lace, 50 units, because the border is 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 units; the red lace and the blue lace are too short.

Challenge: 'She decides to use two different coloured laces. How much lace of each kind will be needed to cover the entire border?' Turn on Two laces, lay the first lace, cut it, then lay a lace of a different colour to finish the border. Answer: any two lengths that make 50 units in all and fit the reels are right, for example 30 units of red lace for the two long sides and 20 units of blue lace for the two short sides, because 30 + 20 = 50, or 25 units of blue lace and 25 units of red lace. Your answer may differ. Next stop: the name for the length of the border.

hint_ladder.text: What does the lace have to go round? Look at the edge of the quilt, all the way round.
Count the lace units along one side of the quilt, one unit for each patch side. Then count the next side.
The long side is 15 units and the short side is 10 units. How many long sides and how many short sides does the border have? Add them all.
15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50. The border is 50 units, so the lace must be 50 units or more. The tool lays the first side so you can see it.

student_does: Look at Grandmother's quilt and the three lace reels from the story. She wants to put lace all the way round the edge of the quilt. Tap the reel you think will go all the way round, then press Next.

Lay each lace along the border from the top left corner and watch where it ends, count the units on each side, count the border of a small practice quilt edge by edge, and see why counting the patches along the border is not the same as counting the lace units.

Answer Grandmother's own questions from the story: Tick the lace option that would cover the entire border of the quilt. She decides to use two different coloured laces. How much lace of each kind will be needed to cover the entire border? Cut two laces that go all the way round.

content.publication_text: Find the perimeter of the following shapes. All sides of the following shapes are equal. $(a)$ the shape on the left, with a side of $4\text{ cm}$; $(b)$ the shape on the right, with a side of $5\text{ cm}$

content.text:
1. $(a)$ The shape on the left has $5$ sides, and every side is $4\text{ cm}$.
2. Add the sides: $4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20$.
3. All the sides are equal, so multiply: $5 \times 4 = 20$. The perimeter is $20\text{ cm}$.
4. $(b)$ The shape on the right has $4$ sides, and every side is $5\text{ cm}$.
5. Add the sides: $5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
6. All the sides are equal, so multiply: $4 \times 5 = 20$. The perimeter is $20\text{ cm}$.
7. Check: for each shape, adding and multiplying give the same number.
Answer: $(a)$: $20\text{ cm}$; $(b)$: $20\text{ cm}$
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.title: Tile the Table
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Tile the Table

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S5.T5.C13.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Grandmother's Quilt, the rug (15 by 6), Tables 1 to 4, the notebooks question, Preetha's desk (9 by 6). Practice values added: trays 7 by 2 and 5 by 3, a table top 60 cm by 30 cm (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student finds which shapes cover a surface with no gaps and no overlaps, and says the area of a region as the number of tiles that cover it, named in the unit of the tile.
- Out of scope: the rule length × breadth, square cm, comparing two regions, perimeter.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- A wooden worktable seen from above. A bare table top, 7 squares long and 2 broad (each square place about 80 px), lies in the middle. A wooden tray along the bottom holds four loose tiles about 70 px across: a yellow triangle, a blue circle, a green square and a pink rectangle (1 square wide, 2 tall).
- Instruction line: "Which shapes can cover the table top with no gaps and no overlaps? Make a guess."
- The child is invited to tick the shapes they think will work.

2. Scene and Objects
- Table top on a wooden worktable photo, top view: light wood, the largest object; faint outlines show the places for the chosen tile.
- Tiles: glossy flat tiles. Triangle: half a square cut corner to corner, 2 per place. Circle: as wide as one place, so gaps stay. Square: 1 place. Rectangle: 1 wide, 2 tall.
- Chips: a tile counter with the name, for example "12 squares", and the goal chip of the activity. Two small round buttons at the table corners: Gaps (empty wood glows orange) and Fill the rest.

3. Main Interaction
- Tap a tile in the tray to pick it. Tap an empty place to drop a tile (it snaps in with a small bounce) or drag across places to drop one in each. Fill the rest covers all empty places. Tap a placed tile to remove it. A tile dropped on a covered place blinks and slides back.
- Counting: tap a tile for the next number badge (1, 2, 3 ...), or drag along a row to count the row. Number dial: 1 to 3 wheels, swipe up or down.
- Bottom buttons (at most 3): Hint, Reset (clears this step), Check, which becomes Next.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Cover the tray with each shape and look for gaps." Goal chip: "Try all 4 shapes". Setup: a tray 7 long and 2 broad (practice values). Guess: the child ticks the shapes they think cover the tray with no gaps and no overlaps. The child covers the tray with each shape in turn. Result: squares (14), triangles (28) and rectangles (7) fit; circles (14) leave round gaps and Gaps turns on. Strip: "Triangles, squares and rectangles cover the tray. Circles leave gaps." Help: guided, places drawn.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Cover the tray with squares and count them." Goal chip: "Find the area". Setup: a tray 5 long and 3 broad (practice values). Guess: "How many squares will cover it? Tap one: 8, 15 or 16." The child covers it row by row. Result: counter "15 squares", strip "3 rows of 5 squares: 3 × 5 = 15. The area of the tray is 15 square units." Help: guided, each row numbered as it fills.
- Activity 3 (guided, then free). Goal line: "Now cover the same tray with triangles." Goal chip: "Same tray, new tile". Setup: the same 5 by 3 tray with the 15 squares drawn faintly under the triangles. Guess: "Will it need fewer triangles, the same number, or more than squares? Tap one." The child covers it with triangles. Result: "30 triangles", strip "Each square is 2 triangles: 15 × 2 = 30. The tray is the same: 15 square units, or 30 triangle units." Help: the faint squares show the cuts, no row numbers.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Preetha and Adrit's grandmother is making a rug with square patches. The picture below shows the rug. How many patches have they used to make this?" Goal chip: "Count the patches". Setup: a rug of red and yellow check patches with a fringe, 15 patches in a row, 6 rows. The child counts by taps or by dragging along a row and sets the dial. Guess: the dial may be set first; nothing shows until Check. Result: "6 rows of 15 patches: 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 90, or 6 × 15 = 90." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2, four steps, on four table tops in a row, already covered: Table 1 triangles (5 by 2 squares, each cut in 2), Table 2 circles (4 by 2), Table 3 squares (4 by 2), Table 4 rectangles (3 by 4). Goal chip: "Tables 1 to 4". Each answer is the child's own commit before Check. Step 2a goal line: "Preetha and Adrit are trying to cover their table with different shapes. Preetha covered it with triangles and circles. Adrit covered with squares and rectangles. They found that ___, ___ and ___ shapes cover the top of the table without gaps and overlaps. ___ shape leaves gaps." The child drags the chips Triangle, Circle, Square, Rectangle into the blanks; right: Triangle, Square, Rectangle in any order, then Circle. Step 2b: "Do circles tile? Can we use them to cover a region?" Table 2 comes forward with Gaps on; the child taps Yes or No; right: No, strip "No. Circles leave gaps, so they do not tile." Step 2c: "___ triangles cover Table 1. ___ squares cover Table 3. ___ rectangles cover Table 4." The child counts and sets 3 dials; right: 20, 8, 12; strip "Table 1: 5 × 2 = 10 squares, each cut in 2, 10 × 2 = 20. Table 3: 4 × 2 = 8. Table 4: 3 × 4 = 12." Step 2d: "The area of Table 1 is ___ triangle units. The area of Table 3 is ___ square units. The area of Table 4 is ___ rectangle units." The counts become tags 20, 8 and 12; the child drags each to its sentence. Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (practice values for the sizes). Goal line: "Now, try to cover the top of your table without gaps and overlaps with the following objects of same size. (a) Notebooks (b) Lunch boxes (c) Pencil boxes (d) Maths books. Which of the above objects covered the region completely?" Goal chip: "Which objects cover?" Setup: a table top 60 cm by 30 cm; four top-view photos: notebook 20 cm by 15 cm, lunch box 15 cm by 10 cm, pencil box 20 cm by 10 cm, maths book 30 cm by 15 cm. Guess: the child ticks the objects they think cover it. The child lays each object, then Fill the rest. Result: notebooks 6, lunch boxes 12, pencil boxes 9, maths books 4; all cover it. Strip: "All four are rectangles, and rectangles tile. Notebooks: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 in a row and 30 ÷ 15 = 2 rows, 3 × 2 = 6. Your own table may give a different answer." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "Look at the different tiles on her desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. (a) Green triangles ___ (b) Red triangles ___ (c) Blue squares ___" Goal chip: "Cover the desk". Setup: Preetha's desk, a white top of 9 columns by 6 rows of equal squares, and three tiles at true size: a blue square (1 square), a green triangle (half a square), a red triangle (two sides of 3 squares meeting in a corner). Guess: "Which tile will you need the most of? Tap blue, green or red." The child covers the desk with each tile; two red triangles snap into a 3 by 3 square. Then 3 dials. Right: (a) 108, (b) 12, (c) 54. Strip: "The desk has 9 × 6 = 54 squares. Blue squares: 54. Green triangles: 54 × 2 = 108. Two red triangles make a 3 by 3 square, the desk holds 3 × 2 = 6 of them: 6 × 2 = 12." Help: independent.

5. Mathematical Understanding
- Tiles meet edge to edge or leave gaps. The area is the count of tiles, named with the tile; one tray covered by squares and then triangles shows the count depends on the tile.
- Rules in the child's words: "Squares, rectangles and triangles tile. Circles leave gaps." "The area is the number of tiles that cover the region." "A different tile gives a different count."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce and the strip shows the why. Wrong answer: red strip, small shake, one friendly line; retry is free, no scores. Confetti only on the end screen. Guesses are never marked wrong: a plain strip says "You guessed X. The answer is Y."
- Mistake: tile put on a covered place -> "This tile overlaps another one. Each tile needs its own place." The covered tile blinks.
- Mistake: Yes for circles -> "Look at the gaps between the circles. Circles leave gaps, so they do not tile." Gaps turns on.
- Mistake: 10 for Table 1 -> "10 is the number of squares. Count the triangles." The cut lines show. A tag on the wrong sentence -> "Table 3 is covered by squares. Use the number of squares."
- Mistake: 54 for red -> "A red triangle is bigger than a square. Two red triangles make a 3 by 3 square." A 3 by 3 block glows.
- Hints, three levels: (1) "Are there gaps between the tiles? Do any tiles lie on top of each other?" or "How many tiles are in one row, and how many rows?" (2) the empty wood glows, or the first row is numbered; (3) "Squares, rectangles and triangles fit edge to edge, circles do not." or "Tiles in a row times rows, for example 3 rows of 5: 3 × 5 = 15." Desk: "9 × 6 = 54 squares. A green triangle is half a square, so double 54."
- Edge case: a single triangle in a place leaves half of it empty and Gaps lights it.

7. Ending
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Squares, rectangles and triangles tile. Circles leave gaps." "The area is the number of tiles that cover the region." "A different tile gives a different count." Think and talk: "The same desk needs 54 squares or 108 triangles. Why is the number different?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: top-view wooden table photo; yellow triangle, blue circle, green square and pink rectangle tile cut-outs; red and yellow check rug with fringe; top-view photos of a notebook, a lunch box, a pencil box and a maths book. The desk grid, counters and dials are drawn in code.
- Language: English only; unit words "square units", "triangle units", "rectangle units".

tool_config.idea: Find out which shapes cover a surface with no gaps and no overlaps, and count the tiles that cover a region as its area in the unit of the tile: triangles, squares and rectangles tile and circles leave gaps, and the same region needs a different number of different tiles.
tool_config.title: Tile the Table
tool_config.screen: The table corner of Grandmother's patchwork room, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Four table tops stand in a row, Table 1, Table 2, Table 3 and Table 4, as in your maths book, and the table being covered is the largest thing on screen, in the middle. Table 1 takes triangles (each square of a 5 by 2 top is cut from corner to corner into 2 triangles), Table 2 takes circles (a 4 by 2 top), Table 3 takes squares (a 4 by 2 top) and Table 4 takes rectangles (a 3 by 4 top). Preetha's desk is a 9 by 6 grid of equal squares with three tiles for it: a blue square, a green triangle that is half a square and a red triangle whose two shorter sides are each 3 squares long. A tile shelf at the side holds a triangle, a circle, a square and a rectangle. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a tile on the shelf and then tap places on the table to put the tile down; a Fill the rest button that repeats the tile over the empty places; an Undo button; a Gaps glow that turns the empty spaces between tiles soft orange; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the table in front), Reset (returns all the tables and the desk), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a tile counter with the name of the tile (for example 20 triangles), a note when there are gaps or overlaps, the area sentence (for example The area of Table 1 is 20 triangle units), and a card number out of 7.
feedback: A tile snaps into the next free place and the counter shows the number and the name of the tile, for example 20 triangles. When the table is full the tool says: No gaps and no overlaps, this tile covers the table.
With circles the Gaps glow lights the empty spaces and the tool says: There are gaps between the circles, so circles do not tile.
The area sentence appears when a table is full, for example: 20 triangles cover Table 1, so its area is 20 triangle units.
On the desk, a tile that is put over another one blinks softly in amber and the tool says: This tile overlaps another one. A tile needs its own place.
A wrong count shows a soft amber note and never a red cross, and the tool names the number it expected only after the second try.
tool_config.done_when: Tables 1, 3 and 4 are covered and counted, the circles have been tried on Table 2, the small tray has been counted in squares and in triangles, the sentences of the four tables are complete, and the desk is covered with each of the three tiles.

challenges: Card 1: pick the triangle and cover Table 1. How many triangles cover it? Answer: 20 triangles, because the table has 5 by 2 squares, 10 squares, and each square is 2 triangles, 10 × 2 = 20. So the area of Table 1 is 20 triangle units.
Card 2: pick the square and cover Table 3. How many squares cover it? Answer: 8 squares, because 4 × 2 = 8. The area of Table 3 is 8 square units.
Card 3: pick the rectangle and cover Table 4. How many rectangles cover it? Answer: 12 rectangles, because 3 × 4 = 12. The area of Table 4 is 12 rectangle units.
Card 4: pick the circle and cover Table 2, then press Gaps. What do you see? Answer: 8 circles fit, 4 in a row and 2 rows, but there are gaps between them, so circles do not tile.

Card 5 (practice values): a tray of 6 squares by 4 squares. Cover it with square tiles, then with triangle tiles, each square cut from corner to corner. Answer: 24 squares, because 6 × 4 = 24, and 48 triangles, because 24 × 2 = 48. The tray did not change, only the tile did.

Challenge: 'They found that ___, ___ and ___ shapes cover the top of the table without gaps and overlaps. ___ shape leaves gaps. ___ triangles cover Table 1. ___ squares cover Table 3. ___ rectangles cover Table 4. The area of Table 1 is ___ triangle units. The area of Table 3 is ___ square units. The area of Table 4 is ___ rectangle units.' Answer: triangle, square and rectangle shapes cover the table, and the circle shape leaves gaps. 20 triangles, 8 squares and 12 rectangles, so the areas are 20 triangle units, 8 square units and 12 rectangle units.

Challenge: 'Look at the different tiles on her desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. (a) Green triangles (b) Red triangles (c) Blue squares.' Cover the desk with each tile in turn. Answer: (a) 108 green triangles, because the desk has 9 × 6 = 54 squares and 54 × 2 = 108; (b) 12 red triangles, because 2 red triangles make a square 3 by 3 and the desk holds 6 of them, 6 × 2 = 12; (c) 54 blue squares.

hint_ladder.text: What does the table need? Look for gaps between the tiles and for tiles that lie on top of each other.
Count the tiles in one row, then count the rows. How many tiles are there in all?
Say the area with the name of the tile, for example 20 triangles make 20 triangle units. A different tile gives a different number.
For the desk: 9 × 6 = 54 squares. Each square is 2 green triangles, 54 × 2 = 108. The tool fills the first row so you can count.

Then cover Preetha's desk with the green triangles, the red triangles and the blue squares.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Preetha covers a table top with circles and Adrit covers one with squares. Whose table top will have gaps? A tile is a shape used to cover a surface. Tiles must fit together with no gaps and no overlaps. Squares fit edge to edge with no gaps. Rectangles fit the same way. Triangles fit too: one table top in your maths book is covered by triangles with no gaps. Circles do not tile. Between round tiles there are always gaps, and to close the gaps the circles would have to overlap. Rule: squares, rectangles and triangles tile a surface; circles leave gaps. 1. content.text: Preetha and Adrit's grandmother is making a rug with square patches. The picture below shows the rug. How many patches have they used to make this?
content.q_figure: A rug made of square patches in alternate red and yellow colours.
content.question: Preetha and Adrit's grandmother is making a rug with square patches. The picture below shows the rug. How many patches have they used to make this?
content.question_tex: Preetha and Adrit's grandmother is making a rug with square patches. The picture below shows the rug. How many patches have they used to make this?
content.publication_text: Preetha and Adrit's grandmother is making a rug with square patches. The picture below shows the rug. How many patches have they used to make this?

content.text:
1. Look at the rug. The patches are in rows, and every row has the same number of patches.
2. Count the rows: there are $6$ rows.
3. Count the patches in one row: there are $15$ patches.
4. Add the rows: $15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 90$. Or multiply: $6 \times 15 = 90$.
5. Check by columns: there are $15$ columns of $6$ patches, and $15 \times 6 = 90$.
Answer: $90$ patches

content.text:
1. Look at Table $2$. It is covered by $8$ circles, $4$ in a row and $2$ rows.
2. There are gaps between the circles and at the edges of the table.
3. To close the gaps the circles would have to overlap each other.
4. A shape tiles only when there are no gaps and no overlaps, so circles do not tile.
[Image: Tiles and Tables: Ans4: solution]
5. Check: squares, rectangles and triangles left no gaps, but the circles did.
Answer: No. Circles leave gaps, so they do not tile and cannot cover a region without gaps or overlaps.

content.text: Preetha is playing with tiles. She covers her desk with different shapes as shown below. Look at the different tiles on her desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. $(a)$ Green triangles $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$; $(b)$ Red triangles $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$; $(c)$ Blue squares $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$
content.q_figure: A desk drawn as a grid of equal squares, with three tiles beside it: a blue square tile the size of one grid square, a green triangle tile that is a grid square cut from corner to corner, and a red triangle tile whose two shorter sides are each as long as 3 grid squares.
content.question: Preetha is playing with tiles. She covers her desk with different shapes as shown below. Look at the different tiles on her desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. (a) Green triangles ___; (b) Red triangles ___; (c) Blue squares ___

Look at the different tiles on her desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. $(a)$ Green triangles $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$; $(b)$ Red triangles $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$; $(c)$ Blue squares $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$
content.publication_text: Preetha is playing with tiles. She covers her desk with different shapes as shown below. Look at the different tiles on her desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. $(a)$ Green triangles $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$; $(b)$ Red triangles $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$; $(c)$ Blue squares $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$

content.text:
1. Count the squares of the desk: $9$ squares in a row and $6$ rows, $9 \times 6 = 54$ squares.
2. $(a)$ A green triangle is half a square, so $2$ green triangles cover $1$ square.
3. $54 \times 2 = 108$ green triangles cover the desk.
4. $(b)$: $2$ red triangles put together make a square $3$ squares long and $3$ squares broad, which is $9$ squares.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
5. The desk holds $9 \div 3 = 3$ of these big squares in a row and $6 \div 3 = 2$ rows, so $3 \times 2 = 6$ big squares.
6. Each big square is $2$ red triangles: $6 \times 2 = 12$ red triangles cover the desk.
7. $(c)$ A blue square is $1$ square, so $54$ blue squares cover the desk.
8. Check: $1$ red triangle covers $9$ green triangles, and $12 \times 9 = 108$, the same as the green count.
Answer: $(a)$: $108$ green triangles; $(b)$: $12$ red triangles; $(c)$: $54$ blue squares
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.title: Grid Area
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Grid Area

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S8.T8.C30.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Grandmother's Quilt, Comparing Shapes: rectangles A (3 by 4), B (2 by 4), C (2 by 5), the gardens (A 2 by 5, B 4 by 3), the palm and the leaves. Practice values added: cut-outs D 6 by 2, E 8 by 4, F 3 by 5, a house of 12 square cm, leaves of 30, 18, 24 square cm (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student compares two areas by laying one shape on the other when one fits inside, and by counting the same unit squares on a grid when neither fits, counting two half squares as one.
- Out of scope: the rule length × breadth, perimeter, area of a triangle by a rule.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- A craft table seen from above. A grid sheet of 1 cm squares lies in the middle, 15 columns by 12 rows, each square about 36 px. Beside it lie two paper cut-outs: a light blue D and a larger orange E.
- Instruction line: "Which paper has the larger area, D or E? Make a guess."
- The child is invited to tap D or E.

2. Scene and Objects
- Grid sheet: thin pale blue lines, a key square marked "1 cm" and "1 unit square", on a light wooden craft table photo.
- Paper cut-outs: coloured paper with a slight shadow and a letter. Practice: D light blue 6 long and 2 broad, E orange 8 by 4, F green 3 by 5. Book shapes: A yellow 3 by 4, B pink 2 by 4, C purple 2 by 5.
- Chips: a counter such as "D: 12" and the activity's goal chip.

3. Main Interaction
- Drag a cut-out onto another: on release its top left corner lines up with the other's. If it fits inside, it clicks in; if not, the part that sticks out glows orange.
- Drag a cut-out onto the grid: it snaps to whole squares. Tap a square, drag across squares or tap a row to count (squares turn orange, counter goes up).
- A half square is a square cut corner to corner. Drag one half square onto another: they join into 1 whole square.
- Trace pad: draw a closed outline on the grid with a finger. Squares fully inside turn pale orange; squares the line crosses are hatched part squares.
- Number dial: 1 to 3 wheels, swipe up or down, "square cm" printed beside it.
- Bottom buttons (at most 3): Hint, Reset (returns the shapes of this step), Check, which becomes Next.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Lay D on E. Does D fit inside?" Goal chip: "Lay one on the other". Setup: D (6 by 2) and E (8 by 4), practice values. Guess: the child taps the one with the larger area. The child drags D onto E. Result: D clicks inside E, strip "D fits inside E, so the area of E is larger." Help: guided, a corner dot shows where the corners meet.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Lay D on F. Then count the squares." Goal chip: "Count to compare". Setup: D (6 by 2) and F (3 by 5). Guess: "Which has the larger area? Tap D, F or Can't tell by laying." The child lays D on F: D sticks out sideways, F sticks out at the top, strip "Neither shape fits inside the other. Count unit squares." The child drags both onto the grid and counts row by row. Result: "D: 2 rows of 6, 6 × 2 = 12. F: 5 rows of 3, 3 × 5 = 15. F has the larger area, though D is longer." Help: guided, rows numbered.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Count the whole squares. Then put the half squares in pairs." Goal chip: "Find the area". Setup: a house on the grid, 4 columns wide: 2 rows of 4 whole squares, then a roof whose lower row is a half square, 2 whole squares and a half square, and whose top row is 2 half squares (10 whole and 4 half squares). Guess: "How many square cm is the house? Tap one: 10, 12 or 14." The child counts the whole squares, then joins the half squares in pairs. Result: "10 whole squares. 4 half squares make 2 squares, 4 ÷ 2 = 2. 10 + 2 = 12. The area is 12 square cm." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (book questions in order, on A, B and C). Goal line: "Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area." Goal chip: "A, B or C?" Setup: cut-outs A, B, C on the table, no grid. Guess: the child taps the one they think is largest. Step 1a: "Do you see that the area of rectangle A is larger than that of B? What about B and C?" The child lays B on A and B on C (B fits inside both), then taps Yes and Yes. Step 1b: "Which shape has a larger area among A and C? How will you find out?" The child lays A on C (neither fits) and taps "Count unit squares on a grid" among 3 method chips. Step 1c: "Let us put these rectangles on a square grid. Now, can you identify the rectangle that has the largest area?" The child drags A, B, C onto a grid of 11 columns by 5 rows, counts, and taps the largest. Result: "A has 3 × 4 = 12 unit squares, C has 2 × 5 = 10 and B has 2 × 4 = 8. 12 is the most, so A has the largest area." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid. Share your observations. Area of Garden A: ___ square cm. Area of Garden B: ___ square cm." Goal chip: "Two gardens". Setup: a grid 7 columns by 6 rows of 1 cm squares: garden A green, 2 wide and 5 tall; a pale strip 1 square wide beside it, part of neither garden; garden B green, 4 wide and 3 tall. Guess: the child taps the garden they think is larger. The child counts each garden by rows and sets two dials: 10 and 12. Then taps "Garden B is larger by 2 square cm" among 3 chips. Result: "Garden A: 5 rows of 2, 5 × 2 = 10. Garden B: 3 rows of 4, 3 × 4 = 12. 12 − 10 = 2, so garden B is larger by 2 square cm. The pale strip is part of neither garden." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Trace your palm on the square grid given below and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?" Goal chip: "Trace and count". Setup: an empty grid of 15 by 12 squares. Guess: the child taps "Mine" or "My friend's" as the bigger palm. The child draws a palm outline, counts the whole squares and joins the part squares in pairs (a lone part square is left out); a friend does the same in another colour. Result: the strip shows the real numbers, for example "54 whole squares and 12 part squares: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, 54 + 6 = 60. About 60 square cm. 60 is more than 48, so this palm is bigger." The child taps who is bigger. Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4 (practice values). Goal line: "Collect leaves of different kinds. Put them on a square grid and find their area. (a) Name the leaf with the largest area. (b) Name the leaf with the smallest area." Goal chip: "Leaves P, Q, R". Setup: three leaf photos P, Q, R. The outline of each, drawn in code over the photo, gives exactly P 24 whole and 12 part squares, Q 12 whole and 12 part, R 18 whole and 12 part (the builder checks). Guess: the child taps the leaf they think is largest. The child drags each leaf to the grid, counts, joins the part squares in pairs, then taps the largest leaf for (a) and the smallest for (b). Result: "P: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, 24 + 6 = 30. R: 18 + 6 = 24. Q: 12 + 6 = 18. The largest is leaf P and the smallest is leaf Q." Help: independent.

5. Mathematical Understanding
- Laying shows that a shape that fits inside the other has the smaller area, and that long is not the same as large. When neither fits, counting the same small squares decides. Two half squares make one whole square.
- Rules in the child's words: "If one fits inside the other, it has the smaller area." "If neither fits, count the same unit squares." "The area is the number of unit squares it covers."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce and the strip shows the why. Wrong answer: red strip, small shake, one friendly line; retry is free, no scores. Confetti only on the end screen. Guesses are never marked wrong: a plain strip says "You guessed X. The answer is Y."
- Mistake: C is larger because it is taller -> "C is taller, but A is wider. Count the squares of each." Both sides pulse. B larger than A -> "B fits inside A. The shape that fits inside has the smaller area."
- Mistake: counts the pale strip -> "The pale strip is not part of a garden. Do not count it." A square tapped twice -> "You counted this square already."
- Mistake: 14 for the house -> "Two half squares make 1 square, not 2." 10 -> "The half squares are part of the house. Put them in pairs." The pairs link.
- Hints, three levels: (1) "Does one shape fit inside the other? Try laying one on the other." or "What can you count that is the same size in both?" (2) the first row is numbered, or the half squares link in pairs; (3) "A is 3 columns and 4 rows: 3 × 4 = 12. C is 2 columns and 5 rows: 2 × 5 = 10."
- Edge cases: equal areas ("Same area: 12 and 12"); a shape fits inside even when edges touch; an open outline asks "Close the outline."

7. Ending
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "If one shape fits inside the other, it has the smaller area." "If neither fits, count the same unit squares." "Two half squares make one whole square." Think and talk: "Is the longer rectangle always the one with the larger area? Why not?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: top-view wood craft table photo; paper texture; three leaf photos with clean edges (mango-type, round, narrow). Grid sheet, house, gardens, rectangles and outlines in code.
- Language: English only.

tool_config.idea: Compare areas by laying shapes on each other when one fits inside the other, and by counting unit squares on a square grid when neither fits inside the other, so that the unit square becomes the measure of area.
tool_config.title: Grid Area
tool_config.screen: A patchwork board in Grandmother's room, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A square grid mat of equal unit squares lies on the table and is the largest thing on screen, with a key square marked 1 unit square and, for the gardens, 1 cm. Beside it lie paper cut-outs: rectangle A (yellow, 3 squares wide and 4 tall), rectangle B (pink, 2 wide and 4 tall) and rectangle C (purple, 2 wide and 5 tall), as in your maths book. A second board shows the two gardens of your maths book on a grid of 1 cm squares: garden A (green, 2 wide and 5 tall) and garden B (green, 4 wide and 3 tall) with a pale strip one square wide that belongs to neither. A trace pad is an empty grid on which a finger draws an outline, for the palm and the leaf. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a cut-out onto another one to overlay it and see whether it fits inside; drag a cut-out onto the grid; tap a square to count it, and it turns orange and the counter goes up; a Show unit squares switch; on the trace pad, draw the outline and tap the whole squares inside it and the part squares that are more than half covered; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (returns the shapes of this step), Reset (clears the board), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the unit squares counted for each shape (for example A 12), a note saying whether one shape fits inside the other, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: A cut-out that fits inside another one clicks into place and the tool says: B fits inside A, so the area of A is larger. A cut-out that does not fit stays half over the edge and the tool says: Neither shape fits inside the other. Count unit squares.
Each tapped square turns orange and the counter goes up by one. The count is shown with the name of the shape, for example A has 12 unit squares.
On the trace pad a whole square tapped inside the outline counts 1, and two part squares count together as 1; the tool shows the total and says it is an approximate area.
When two shapes are counted the tool compares them: 12 is more than 10, so A has the larger area.
A wrong count shows a soft amber note and never a red cross, and the tool names the number it expected only after the second try.
tool_config.done_when: The student has seen that B fits inside A and inside C, has seen that A and C cannot be settled by laying one on the other, has counted A, B and C and the two gardens on the grid, has counted the two practice rectangles and the triangle, and has traced a palm or a leaf and found an approximate area.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: drag B onto A, then onto C. What do you see? Answer: B fits inside A and B fits inside C, so A has a larger area than B and C has a larger area than B.
Card 2: drag A onto C. Does one fit inside the other? Answer: no. A is wider than C, but C is taller than A, so laying one on the other does not tell us which area is larger.
Card 3: put A and C on the grid and count their unit squares. Answer: A has 3 × 4 = 12 unit squares and C has 2 × 5 = 10 unit squares, so A has the larger area.

Card 4 (practice values): a rectangle 7 squares long and 2 broad and a rectangle 4 squares long and 4 broad. Count the squares of each. Answer: 2 × 7 = 14 squares and 4 × 4 = 16 squares, so the 4 by 4 rectangle has the larger area, though it is the shorter one.

Card 5 (practice values): a triangle on a grid of 1 cm squares with two sides 4 squares long. Count the whole squares and the half squares. Answer: 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 ÷ 2 = 2, so the area is 6 + 2 = 8 square cm.
Challenge: 'Which of the above rectangles has the largest area?' Put A, B and C on the square grid and count. Answer: A has 12 unit squares, B has 8 and C has 10, so A has the largest area.

Challenge: 'Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid. Area of Garden A = ___ cm square. Area of Garden B = ___ cm square.' Count the squares of each garden. Answer: garden A is 2 × 5 = 10 square cm and garden B is 4 × 3 = 12 square cm, so garden B has the larger area. The pale strip belongs to neither garden.

hint_ladder.text: Which shapes are you comparing? Try laying one on the other first.
If one shape does not fit inside the other, put both on the grid and count the same small squares in each.
Count the squares in one row, then count the rows, and multiply. Do this for each shape.
A is 3 columns and 4 rows, so 3 × 4 = 12. C is 2 columns and 5 rows, so 2 × 5 = 10. The tool counts the first row so you can see it.

content.text:
Worked example: Mat P is 7 squares long and 2 squares broad. Mat Q is 4 squares long and 4 squares broad. Which mat has the larger area?
1. Lay mat Q on mat P. Q is shorter than P in length, but Q is broader. Neither mat fits inside the other, so laying them does not settle it.
2. Cover both with the same square tiles and count. Mat P has 2 rows of 7 squares: 2 × 7 = 14 squares.
3. Mat Q has 4 rows of 4 squares: 4 × 4 = 16 squares.
4. 16 is more than 14, so mat Q has the larger area.
5. Check: Q is not the longer mat, yet it has the larger area, so length alone cannot decide.
Answer: Mat Q has the larger area: 16 squares is more than 14 squares

media.teaching_notes: 1. Trace the three rectangles on paper and cut them out. 2. Lay B on A: B fits inside A, so the area of A is larger than the area of B. 3. Lay B on C: B fits inside C, so the area of C is larger than the area of B. So B is the smallest. 4. Lay A on C: neither fits inside the other, because A is wider and C is taller. Cutting alone does not tell us. 5. Put the rectangles on a square grid and count the unit squares: A has 3 × 4 = 12, C has 2 × 5 = 10 and B has 2 × 4 = 8. 6. 12 is the most, so A has the largest area. 7. Check: 12 is more than 10, and 10 is more than 8. Answer: A has the largest area: 12 unit squares, against 10 for C and 8 for B.

content.text: Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area.
content.q_figure: Three rectangles side by side: A yellow, B pink and C purple, with A the widest and C the tallest, drawn without a grid.
content.question: Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area.
content.book_number: Comparing Shapes: which rectangle is largest
content.question_tex: Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area.
content.publication_text: Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area.

content.text:
1. Trace the three rectangles on paper and cut them out.
2. Lay $B$ on $A$: $B$ fits inside $A$, so the area of $A$ is larger than the area of $B$.
3. Lay $B$ on $C$: $B$ fits inside $C$, so the area of $C$ is larger than the area of $B$. So $B$ is the smallest.
4. Lay $A$ on $C$: neither fits inside the other, because $A$ is wider and $C$ is taller. Cutting alone does not tell us.
[Image: Comparing Shapes: Ans1: solution]
5. Put the rectangles on a square grid and count the unit squares: $A$ has $3 \times 4 = 12$, $C$ has $2 \times 5 = 10$ and $B$ has $2 \times 4 = 8$.
6. $12$ is the most, so $A$ has the largest area.
7. Check: $12$ is more than $10$, and $10$ is more than $8$.
Answer: $A$ has the largest area: $12\text{ unit}$ squares, against $10$ for $C$ and $8$ for $B$.
[Image: Comparing Shapes: Ans1: solution (continued)]

1. Lay $A$ on $C$. $A$ is wider than $C$, but $C$ is taller than $A$, so neither fits inside the other.
2. We cannot tell by laying one on the other, so put both on a square grid.
3. Count the unit squares of $A$: $3$ columns and $4$ rows, $3 \times 4 = 12$.
4. Count the unit squares of $C$: $2$ columns and $5$ rows, $2 \times 5 = 10$.
[Image: Comparing Shapes: Ans3: solution]
5. $12$ is more than $10$, so $A$ has the larger area.
6. Check: count A row by row: $3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12$.
Answer: $A$ has the larger area. Put both on a square grid and count: $A$ has $12\text{ unit}$ squares and $C$ has $10$.

content.text: Let us put these rectangles on a square grid. Now, can you identify the rectangle that has the largest area?

content.publication_text: Let us put these rectangles on a square grid. Now, can you identify the rectangle that has the largest area?

content.text:
1. On the grid every square is $1\text{ unit}$ square, so the area is the number of squares covered.
2. A covers $3$ columns and $4$ rows: $3 \times 4 = 12$ squares.
3. $B$ covers $2$ columns and $4$ rows: $2 \times 4 = 8$ squares.
4. $C$ covers $2$ columns and $5$ rows: $2 \times 5 = 10$ squares.
5. $12$ is more than $10$, and $10$ is more than $8$, so $A$ has the largest area, then $C$, then $B$.
6. Check: count A again by columns: $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$.
Answer: Yes. A covers $12\text{ unit}$ squares, $B$ covers $8$ and $C$ covers $10$, so $A$ has the largest area.

content.text: Trace your palm on the square grid given below and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?

content.question: Trace your palm on the square grid given below and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?

content.text:
1. Put your hand flat on the grid and trace round it with a pencil. Each square of the grid is $1\text{ square cm}$.
2. Count the whole squares inside the outline.
3. Then look at the squares that are only partly inside. Put them together in your mind: two part squares make about $1$ whole square.
4. Add the whole squares and the squares made from the parts. This is the approximate area of your palm.
[Image: Let us do: Ans2: solution]
5. Do the same for your friend's palm and compare the two numbers: the bigger number is the bigger palm.
6. Sample answer with practice values: my palm has $54$ whole squares and $12$ part squares, which make about $6$ whole squares, so the area is about $54 + 6 = 60\text{ square cm}$.
7. My friend's palm is about $48\text{ square cm}$. $60$ is more than $48$, so my palm is bigger. Your answer may differ.
Answer: Sample answer: my palm is about $60\text{ square cm}$ and my friend's is about $48\text{ square cm}$, so my palm is bigger. Your answer may differ.

media.title: Shape Builder
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Shape Builder

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S11.T11.C47.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Grandmother's Quilt, Area and Perimeter Are Different: the mats, Trisha's rectangles, the Let Us Explore shapes, the 9 by 2 shape, the 3 by 3 square and the triangle. Practice values added: 7 by 2, 5 by 4, 10 by 2, perimeter 24 (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that area counts the squares inside a shape and perimeter counts the edges round the outside, so one can stay the same while the other changes.
- Out of scope: the rules length × breadth and 2 × length + 2 × breadth.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- A wooden building board seen from above with a grid of 15 columns by 12 rows of 1 cm squares, each about 40 px, and a 7 by 2 rug of orange patches at the upper left. Two chips above the grid: "Area ?" (orange) and "Perimeter ?" (dark grey).
- Instruction line: "Count the squares inside. Then count the edges round the outside."
- The child is invited to tap Same or Different (the first guess).

2. Scene and Objects
- Wooden board photo, top view, pale grid lines. Patches: orange fabric squares with a thin seam. The outer edges of a shape are a thick dark line.
- Shelf of 3 slots along the bottom; a saved shape shows as a small copy with its numbers, for example "A 20, P 18". Small stage buttons: Save, Clear, Undo.

3. Main Interaction
- Tap a square to place a patch, tap again to remove it; drag across squares to place several. Patches must touch along a whole edge and leave no hole, else a plain note says so.
- The Area and Perimeter chips update live. On shapes the tool shows, trace: drag a finger round the outline; each outer edge passed lights up with a running count, and the number stays on the shape when the loop closes. Drag across a shape to count its squares. Tap a shape to tick it; tap answer chips.
- Bottom buttons (at most 3): Hint, Reset (clears this step), Check, which becomes Next.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Count the squares inside. Then count the edges round the outside." Goal chip: "Area and perimeter". Setup: the 7 by 2 rug; chips show "?". Guess: "Will Area and Perimeter be the same number? Tap Same or Different." The child counts the squares by dragging and traces the outline. Result: "Area 14: 2 rows of 7, 7 × 2 = 14. Perimeter 18: 7 + 2 + 7 + 2 = 18. They are two different measures." Help: guided, squares inside glow orange.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Build two rectangles that each have 20 squares." Goal chip: "Area 20, twice". Setup: faint dotted outlines of 5 by 4, then 10 by 2; the child fills each and presses Save. Guess: after the first save, "Will the next one have the same perimeter? Tap Same or Different." Result: "Both have 20 squares: 5 × 4 = 20, 10 × 2 = 20. The perimeters are 5 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 18 and 10 + 2 + 10 + 2 = 24. Same area, different perimeters." Help: guided, dotted outlines.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Build three different rectangles that each have a perimeter of 24." Goal chip: "Perimeter 24, three times". Setup: empty board. Guess: "Will rectangles with the same perimeter have the same area? Tap Same or Different." The child builds until Perimeter reads 24 and saves; any three different rectangles are right (a turned copy is the same). Result, for example 10 by 2, 9 by 3, 7 by 5: "All three have perimeter 24: 7 + 5 + 7 + 5 = 24. The areas are 20, 27 and 35. Same perimeter, different areas." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (two parts). Part 1a goal line: "The following mats are made of square patches of equal size. How many square patches will be required to cover each mat? Would both mats require an equal or different number of patches? Trace and cut out a small square of the size given below and find the area. (a) Area = ___ Perimeter = ___ (b) Area = ___ Perimeter = ___" Goal chip: "Two mats". Setup: mat (a) 5 long and 2 broad, mat (b) 4 long and 3 broad, empty outlines each with one 1 cm patch at its top left corner. Guess: the child taps Equal or Different for the number of patches. The child fills each mat (Area fills in), traces each outline (Perimeter fills in) and taps Equal or Different again. Right: Different. Result: "Mat (a): 5 × 2 = 10 patches, perimeter 5 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 14 cm. Mat (b): 4 × 3 = 12 patches, perimeter 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 cm. Different patches, same perimeter." Part 1b goal line: "Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?" The child builds Trisha's rectangles, 2 by 3 (Area 6, Perimeter 10) and 3 by 4 (Area 12, Perimeter 14), taps Always true or Not always true, then builds and saves two rectangles where the area goes up and the perimeter does not. Right: Not always true. Result, for example 10 by 1 then 5 by 3: "10 by 1: area 10, perimeter 10 + 1 + 10 + 1 = 22. 5 by 3: area 15, perimeter 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16. The area went up and the perimeter went down, so it is not always true." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss." Goal chip: "Same area". Setup: six green shapes (wide by tall): (a) 6 by 2; (b) a 2 by 5 block with a row of 2 on top, shifted one square left; (c) 3 by 4; (d) 4 by 3; (e) a row of 8; (f) a row of 12. The child ticks the shapes with the same area (the guess) and presses Check; right: (a), (b), (c), (d), (f). Then traces each ticked outline; right: 16, 18, 14, 14, 26. Then taps "Same area, different perimeters" among 3 chips. Result: "These five cover 12 square cm each, but their perimeters 16, 18, 14, 14 and 26 differ." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss." Goal chip: "Same perimeter". Setup: five pink shapes of 7 squares: (a) 3 by 2 with 1 square under its right end; (b) a row of 3 over a 2 by 2 block, sticking out right; (c) a column of 4 with a square on each side of its third square and one right of its top square; (d) a column of 5 with 2 more to the right of its bottom square; (e) a row of 7. The child traces each outline (12, 12, 16, 16, 16), then ticks one group and presses Check, then the other; right: (a) and (b); (c), (d) and (e). Then drags across each shape to count its squares (7) and taps "All areas are 7, the perimeters are not all the same" among 3 chips. Result: "Every shape has an area of 7 square cm, but the perimeter is 12 cm for two shapes and 16 cm for three." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4 (two parts). Part 4a goal line: "Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice? Discuss." Setup: a given green rectangle 9 wide and 2 tall (Area 18, Perimeter 22). The child builds and saves 2 different shapes of exactly 18 squares (a turned 9 by 2 does not count). Result, for example 6 by 3: "All have 18 squares. The perimeters are 22 and 6 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18. Same area, not the same perimeter." Part 4b goal line: "Is the area of shape (a) less than the area of shape (b) given below? Discuss." Setup: (a) a blue square 3 by 3, (b) an orange triangle with a top side of 6 squares and its point 3 squares below the middle. The child counts (a), taps the 6 whole squares of (b), joins its 6 half squares in 3 pairs and taps Yes or No. Right: No. Result: "(a): 3 × 3 = 9. (b): 6 whole squares and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 more, 6 + 3 = 9. The areas are equal." Help: independent.

5. Mathematical Understanding
- Reading both numbers while building shows the child that they move differently.
- Rules in the child's words: "Area counts the squares inside. Perimeter counts the edges round the outside." "The same area can have different perimeters." "A bigger area does not always mean a bigger perimeter."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce and the strip shows the why. Wrong answer: red strip, small shake, one friendly line; retry is free, no scores. Confetti only on the end screen. Guesses are never marked wrong: a plain strip says "You guessed X. The answer is Y."
- Mistake: ticks (e) -> "Shape (e) has 8 squares, not 12. Count its squares again." Its squares light up with a count. Leaves out (f) -> "Count the squares of every shape, even the thin ones."
- Mistake: the loop skips an edge -> "Go all the way round. An edge was left out." It blinks. An inside edge -> "That edge is inside. Count only the outside edges."
- Mistake: a Trisha pair where the perimeter also goes up -> "Here the perimeter went up too. Try a pair where it stays the same or goes down." The given shape turned round -> "That is the same shape turned round. Make a different one."
- Hints, three levels: (1) "What does each number count? Area counts the squares inside. Perimeter counts the edges round the outside." (2) the squares inside glow orange, or the outline runs once round with a counter; (3) "For 5 by 4: 5 × 4 = 20 squares, and 5 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 18 edges." Trisha: "Try 10 by 1, then 5 by 3."
- Edge case: a single patch (Area 1, Perimeter 4).

7. Ending
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Area counts the squares inside. Perimeter counts the edges round the outside." "Shapes with the same area can have different perimeters." "A bigger area does not always mean a bigger perimeter." Think and talk: "Can two rectangles have the same perimeter and different areas? Show one pair." Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: top-view wooden board photo; orange fabric patch texture. Grid, shapes and chips are drawn in code.
- Language: English only.

tool_config.idea: Build shapes on a square grid and read the area and the perimeter side by side, to see that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters, that shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas, and that a bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.
tool_config.title: Shape Builder
tool_config.screen: Grandmother's patchwork board, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A big grid of 15 columns by 12 rows of equal unit squares lies on the table and is the largest thing on screen, with a box of loose unit patches beside it. Two read-outs sit above the grid: Area, the number of squares inside the shape, and Perimeter, the number of edges all the way round it, with the outline of the shape drawn thick. A shelf below the grid keeps up to 3 saved shapes, each with its Area and Perimeter written on it. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a square to place a patch and tap it again to take it away; drag across squares to place several at once; a Save shape button that puts the shape on the shelf; a Show outline switch that lights the outer edges one by one as they are counted; a Clear button; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the grid of this step), Reset (clears the grid and the shelf), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: Area (squares), Perimeter (edges), the saved shapes on the shelf, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: Each patch placed adds 1 to Area, and Perimeter shows the number of outer edges. When a patch is placed the outline redraws, and the tool says for example: Area 16 and Perimeter 20.
When two saved shapes have the same Area the tool says: Same area, different perimeters. When they have the same Perimeter it says: Same perimeter, different areas.
When the student builds a shape that does not match the card, a soft amber note says what is off, for example: This shape has 15 squares. The card asks for 16.
In the Trisha card, after the second pair, the tool says: The area went up from 10 to 12 and the perimeter stayed 14. So a bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.
A wrong tick shows a soft amber note and never a red cross, and it asks the student to count the squares and the outer edges again.
tool_config.done_when: The student has built shapes of one area with different perimeters and shapes of one perimeter with different areas, has found a pair where the area goes up and the perimeter goes down, and has answered Trisha's question, the two Let Us Explore questions and the drawing question with the shapes.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): build a 4 by 4 rectangle, an 8 by 2 rectangle and a 16 by 1 rectangle, and save each one. What do you notice? Answer: all three have an area of 16 square units, because 4 × 4 = 16, 8 × 2 = 16 and 16 × 1 = 16, but the perimeters are different: 16, 20 and 34 units.

Card 2 (practice values): build a 5 by 5, a 7 by 3 and a 9 by 1 rectangle, and save each one. What do you notice? Answer: all three have a perimeter of 20 units, because 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20, 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 and 9 + 1 + 9 + 1 = 20, but the areas are different: 25, 21 and 9 square units.

Card 3 (practice values): build a 1 by 8 rectangle and then a 3 by 3 square. Which number goes up and which goes down? Answer: the area goes up, from 1 × 8 = 8 to 3 × 3 = 9, and the perimeter goes down, from 18 to 12. A bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.

Challenge: 'Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?' Build her two rectangles, 2 squares by 3 and 3 squares by 4, and then try 5 by 2 and 4 by 3. Answer: for her rectangles the area grows from 6 to 12 and the perimeter from 10 to 14, but 5 by 2 and 4 by 3 have areas 10 and 12 and the same perimeter, 14. No, it is not always true.

Challenge: 'Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice?' The six shapes (a) to (f) are on the grid. Answer: (a), (b), (c), (d) and (f) have an area of 12 square cm, and their perimeters are 16, 18, 14, 14 and 26 cm. Shape (e) has an area of 8. The same area can have different perimeters.

Challenge: 'Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice?' The five shapes (a) to (e) are on the grid. Answer: (a) and (b) have a perimeter of 12 cm and (c), (d) and (e) have a perimeter of 16 cm. Every shape has an area of 7 square cm.

Challenge: 'Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice?' The given shape is 9 squares by 2 and has an area of 18. Answer: any shape of exactly 18 squares is right, for example 6 by 3 with a perimeter of 18 cm, or 18 by 1 with a perimeter of 38 cm; the given shape has a perimeter of 22 cm. The perimeters are not all the same. Your answer may differ.

For a 4 by 4 shape: 4 × 4 = 16 squares, and 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 edges. The tool builds it and counts the edges so you can see them.

Challenge: 'Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?' Build her two rectangles, 2 squares by 3 and 3 squares by 4, and then try 5 by 2 and 4 by 3. Answer: for her rectangles the area grows from 6 to 12 and the perimeter from 10 to 14, but 5 by 2 and 4 by 3 have areas 10 and 12 and the same perimeter, 14. No, it is not always true.

Challenge: 'Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice?' The six shapes (a) to (f) are on the grid. Answer: (a), (b), (c), (d) and (f) have an area of 12 square cm, and their perimeters are 16, 18, 14, 14 and 26 cm. Shape (e) has an area of 8. The same area can have different perimeters.

Challenge: 'Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice?' The five shapes (a) to (e) are on the grid. Answer: (a) and (b) have a perimeter of 12 cm and (c), (d) and (e) have a perimeter of 16 cm. Every shape has an area of 7 square cm.

Challenge: 'Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice?' The given shape is 9 squares by 2 and has an area of 18. Answer: any shape of exactly 18 squares is right, for example 6 by 3 with a perimeter of 18 cm, or 18 by 1 with a perimeter of 38 cm; the given shape has a perimeter of 22 cm. The perimeters are not all the same. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
Worked example: Three rectangles are each made of 16 unit squares: 4 by 4, 8 by 2 and 16 by 1. Find the area and the perimeter of each.
1. Areas: 4 × 4 = 16, 8 × 2 = 16 and 16 × 1 = 16. All three have the same area, 16 square units.
2. Perimeter of the 4 by 4 rectangle: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 units.
3. Perimeter of the 8 by 2 rectangle: 8 + 2 + 8 + 2 = 20 units.
4. Perimeter of the 16 by 1 rectangle: 16 + 1 + 16 + 1 = 34 units.
5. Check: 16, 20 and 34 are three different numbers.
Answer: All three have an area of 16 square units, but the perimeters are 16, 20 and 34 units

1. Lay the small patch along mat $(a)$ again and again: it fits $5$ times in a row and $2$ times along the breadth. The patch is $1\text{ cm}$ by $1\text{ cm}$, the same as a $1\text{ cm}$ square of the grids.
2. Mat $(a)$: $2$ rows of $5$ patches, $2 \times 5 = 10$ patches. The area is $10\text{ square cm}$.
3. The perimeter of mat $(a)$: $5 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 14\text{ cm}$.

5. The perimeter of mat $(b)$: $4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14\text{ cm}$.

Answer: $(a)$: $10$ patches, area $10\text{ square cm}$, perimeter $14\text{ cm}$; $(b)$: $12$ patches, area $12\text{ square cm}$, perimeter $14\text{ cm}$. Different numbers of patches.

content.text:
1. Shape $(a)$ is a square $3$ squares wide and $3$ squares tall. Its area is $3 \times 3 = 9$ square units.
2. Shape $(b)$ is a triangle. Count its whole squares row by row: the top row has $4$ whole squares, the next row has $2$ and the last row has $0$: $4 + 2 + 0 = 6$ whole squares.
3. Count its half squares: each row has $2$, so there are $6$ half squares. $2$ half squares make $1$ whole square, so $6 \div 2 = 3$ whole squares.
[Image: Let us do: Ans3: solution]
4. The area of shape $(b)$ is $6 + 3 = 9$ square units.
5. Shape $(a)$ has $9$ and shape $(b)$ has $9$, so the two areas are equal.
6. Check: $9$ is not less than $9$, so the area of $(a)$ is not less than the area of $(b)$.
Answer: No. Shape $(a)$ has $9\text{ unit}$ squares. Shape $(b)$ has $6$ whole squares and $6$ half squares, which is also $9$. The areas are equal.

media.teaching_notes: 1. First rectangle: 2 squares wide and 3 squares tall. Area: 2 × 3 = 6 square units. Perimeter: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10 units. 2. Second rectangle: 3 squares wide and 4 squares tall. Area: 3 × 4 = 12 square units. Perimeter: 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14 units. 3. Here the area grew from 6 to 12 and the perimeter grew from 10 to 14. Trisha is right for these two rectangles. 4. But is it always true? Look at the two mats: the area grew from 10 to 12, and the perimeter stayed 14. 5. Try one more pair. A 1 by 8 rectangle has area 1 × 8 = 8 and perimeter 1 + 8 + 1 + 8 = 18. A 3 by 3 square has area 3 × 3 = 9 and perimeter 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. The area grew and the perimeter became smaller. 6. So a bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter. 7. Check: 18 is more than 12, so the perimeter went down while the area went up. Answer: No, it is not always true. Here both grew (area 6 to 12, perimeter 10 to 14), but the mats have areas 10 and 12 and the same perimeter 14.

content.book_number: Trisha's Rectangles: is it always true
content.question_tex: Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?
content.publication_text: Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?

content.text:
1. First rectangle: $2$ squares wide and $3$ squares tall. Area: $2 \times 3 = 6$ square units. Perimeter: $2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10\text{ units}$.
2. Second rectangle: $3$ squares wide and $4$ squares tall. Area: $3 \times 4 = 12$ square units. Perimeter: $3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14\text{ units}$.
3. Here the area grew from $6$ to $12$ and the perimeter grew from $10$ to $14$. Trisha is right for these two rectangles.
[Image: Trisha's Rectangles: Ans1: solution]
4. But is it always true? Look at the two mats: the area grew from $10$ to $12$, and the perimeter stayed $14$.
5. Try one more pair. $A 1$ by $8$ rectangle has area $1 \times 8 = 8$ and perimeter $1 + 8 + 1 + 8 = 18$. $A 3$ by $3$ square has area $3 \times 3 = 9$ and perimeter $3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12$. The area grew and the perimeter became smaller.
6. So a bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.
7. Check: $18$ is more than $12$, so the perimeter went down while the area went up.
Answer: No, it is not always true. Here both grew (area $6$ to $12$, perimeter $10$ to $14$), but the mats have areas $10$ and $12$ and the same perimeter $14$.

$(b)$: $3$ across the top, $1$ down, $1$ back, $2$ down, $2$ back, $3$ up the left side: $3 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 12\text{ cm}$.

$(c)$: a column of $4$ squares has $4 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 10$ edges round it. Each of the $3$ squares joined to its side hides $1$ edge and shows $3$ new edges, so each adds $2$: $10 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16\text{ cm}$.
$(d)$: $1$ across the top, $4$ down, $2$ across, $1$ down, $3$ back along the bottom, $5$ up the left side: $1 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 5 = 16\text{ cm}$.
$(e)$: a row of $7$ squares has $7 + 1 + 7 + 1 = 16\text{ cm}$.
Shapes $(a)$ and $(b)$ have the same perimeter, $12\text{ cm}$. Shapes $(c)$, $(d)$ and $(e)$ have the same perimeter, $16\text{ cm}$. Tick these.
Notice: all five shapes have the area $7\text{ square cm}$, but the perimeter is $12\text{ cm}$ for two of them and $16\text{ cm}$ for three. The same area can have different perimeters.
